blocks.text: In the Talmud passage (Chulin 59b) mention is made of an עיוא כרכם, "goat of Kerkus." Rashi reads: כרכות, and Karo (on Tur Jore Dea §. 80) throughout: כרכין. Most probably a local reference is indicated here, only כרכם can hardly be determined with certainty; it may mean Kerkusia, Cercusium (biblical כרכמיש*), Jes. 10, 9), Circassia, Kirghizia, Χερχίς [Cherchis] (Sachs: Beiträge etc. no. 2, p. 100); see also Luzzatto on Jes. ibid.; we shall therefore have to keep to the natural-historical features of the animal that are given, [p. 127] which are indeed suited to let the species meant be recognized with some certainty. The עיוא כרכם, it is said, has horns which are הדורות and חרוקות. Of the various explanations of these determinations, among which Rashi, Tosephot, Sal. Adrat, Alfasi and Nissim are divided, we properly hold to the final result set out by the Sch. Aruch (Jore Dea §. 80, 1), according to which הדורות means round horns (not broad, as in the goat) and חרוקות ringed and notched horns.

The gazelle (in Linnaeus: Antilope Dorcas) has thick, round, black-ringed horns shaped like a lyre (Voigt l. c. 1, p. 419), and is probably identical with the עיוא כרכם; the Talmud rightly counts it among the genus of wild animals and accordingly permits the eating of its tallow (§. 22). We add the words of Rosenmüller (Bibl. Alterth. vol. 4, Part 2, p. 171): "The chief characteristic of the antelope genus consists in the nature of the horns, whose bony core or peg is, according to the usual account, solid, without cavity or pores, and which in their outward form are without exception simple and slender, in almost all not flattened but roundish, or variously curved, mostly furnished in their lower part with projecting rings or spiral ridges."
We therefore believe that we are not mistaken in the identification of the animal.

The biblical תאו (5. B. M. 14, 5) Onkelos renders by תורבלא, which the Talmud (Chulin 80a) renders with שור הבר. Maimuni (Kilajim 8, 6) translates שור הבר by שור המדברי, "ox of the wilderness," i.e., the wild, non-domesticated ox. The Maimonidean expression is not identical with the Talmudic שור המדבר (B. Kama 44b), since in the latter passage it designates any ox that has become ownerless (see §. 160). The aurochs is counted among the genus of cattle (§. 19) (Kilajim ibid.), for which reason Rashi's statement (B. Kama 117a) that the aurochs is a חיה is not to be taken in the proper sense of the meaning of the word חיה.

It was caught with snares (ibid.); here the Talmud refers to Jesaias 51, 20, where it says: The תוא lies entangled in snares; on this Kimchi remarks that תוא, through transposition of the letters (as כבש and כשב), is the biblical תאו, but Ibn Esra considers תוא [p. 128] a bird, probably because he finds it strange that the strong aurochs should be caught with snares. According to Aristotle (l. c. 9, 32) it is killed with missiles; at present, when the animal is confined to only a few spots in Russia, it is caught in pits; yet there is no reason to doubt the method of capture stated by the Talmud, since even now the method of capture for many animals differs in different countries; how manifold, e.g., is the manner of catching the whale.

The translation of the biblical word (Deut. 14, 5 and Jes. 51, 20) in Zunz's Bible translation by "buffalo" is wrong, since the latter animal is never called שור הבר, with which תאן is identical; cf. the following article *)

For this animal no name is found in the Talmud, but later authors made use of several names to designate the buffalo, in which one has to think of a kind of provincialism. Thus the Tosephot (Sebachim 113b. s.v. אורזילא) say: ואותם בופלש שאנו קורין ראם, "Those buffaloes which we call Reem," but they themselves add that the buffalo is by no means identical with the ראם, for the latter belongs to the genus of wild animals, whereas the buffalo belongs to the genus of cattle.
Thus there was no special name for the buffalo, and another animal's name was borrowed for it.

Likewise some called the buffalo: [p. 129] שור הבר (Mos. Iserels on Jore Dea §. 28, 4), which, however, is rightly rejected by Alexander Schor (שור תבואות ib. §. 28, 6), since שור הבר is only the aurochs; the addition בר fits the buffalo all the less, since it does not live outdoors like the aurochs, but is kept in stables like other cattle.

Others even call the buffalo by the biblical מריא (Karo on Tur Jore Dea §. 28*), still others call it טור (Taurus) and דוביא (Lorje in Alexander Schor ibid.). One sees from this that the buffalo originally had no distinguishing name, and we should almost assert that it was entirely unknown to the Talmudists, for in Bechoroth 8a, in the specific statement of the gestation period of many animals, the general assertion is made that the large cattle (בהמה גסה) carry for nine months, whereas precisely the buffalo cow carries eleven months (Voigt l. c. 1, p. 429), which the Talmud would certainly not have passed over in silence if the buffalo had been known to it.
Masc. שור and תור (Taurus, Sanhedrin 18b), pl. שורים (B. Kama 14a), and שורים (ibid. 37a).
The suckling calf: עגל הרך (Chulin 122a), then in the first year: עגלה and עגל (Para ib.), in the second year: עגלת בקר (ibid.).
The third-born calf is called: עגלא תילתא (Sabbat 11a**).

The fighting bull is called: שור האיצטדין (B. Kama 39a), and the ox declared by its owner as free property (הפקר): שור המדבר (ibid. 44b), which, incidentally, is of validity only in a regulation of penal law.
